meta.title: Who really said "Freedom is participation in power"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Cicero, on the available evidence. Wikiquote calls it a misquotation with no Latin original, and no one has traced where the English sentence came from.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Freedom is participation in power'?
meta.ogDescription: Attributed to Cicero everywhere, sourced nowhere. Wikiquote: “a misquotation… no reference or source to the Latin original anywhere.”

answer.label: Not Cicero — and no author has ever been traced
answer.authorName: Unknown — no source has been found
answer.sourceLine: We could not find this sentence in Cicero, in any translation of Cicero, or in any dated source at all. Wikiquote’s Talk:Cicero page ↗ lists it among unsourced attributions with the blunt editorial note “This is a misquotation. There is no reference or source to the Latin original anywhere.” It does not appear in Wikiquote’s sourced Cicero page ↗, and Quote Investigator has no article on it ↗. Until someone produces a citation, the honest answer is that nobody knows who wrote it.

source.heading: What we looked for, and did not find
source.excerpt: Freedom is participation in power. (This is a misquotation. There is no reference or source to the Latin original anywhere.)
trail: Wikiquote’s Talk:Cicero page ↗ carries the line in its “Unsourced → Translations” list with the parenthetical verdict: “This is a misquotation. There is no reference or source to the Latin original anywhere.”

Wikiquote’s Sourced and Unsourced policy ↗ defines that list as quotations “widely attributed to the author or work but not sourced to an original work or reputable secondary publication” — i.e. quarantined pending a citation, not endorsed.
We read the whole sourced Wikiquote Cicero page ↗, including its Disputed and Misattributed sections. The sentence is not in any of them.
Searching Quote Investigator for the phrase ↗ returns nothing — the specialists who would normally have traced a saying this widely repeated have not written it up.
source.excerptNote: This is the entry as it stands on Wikiquote’s Talk:Cicero page ↗ — the sentence together with its editors’ verdict. It is the closest thing to a “source” this quotation has.
source.rightsNote: We cannot state a copyright status, because we could not identify the work the sentence comes from or when it was first published. A saying with no traceable origin is not thereby public domain, and we will not assert that it is.

author.name: Marcus Tullius Cicero
author.heading: About Marcus Tullius Cicero
author.metaLine: 106–43 BC · Roman orator, lawyer & consul — credited here, but without evidence
author.bio: Marcus Tullius Cicero was a Roman lawyer, consul and political theorist whose speeches and letters survive in greater volume than those of any other figure of the late Republic. That survival is precisely why he attracts false quotations: an enormous, largely unread corpus makes any invented aphorism feel like it might be in there somewhere. This particular sentence is not.

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: The line circulates as Cicero in civic and political writing, on merchandise, and across every large quotation aggregator. None of them cites a work.

items.why: Wikiquote’s editors ↗ record that no reference or source to a Latin original exists anywhere, and the line is absent from their sourced Cicero page ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: There is no true author to name here yet. What we can say with confidence is what the sentence is not: it is not a translation of anything anyone has been able to find in Cicero.

context.heading: Why it sticks to Cicero
lead: The sentence is a plausible forgery, which is why it survives. Cicero was Rome’s most quotable defender of the republic, and an aphorism defining liberty as a share in governing sounds exactly like something a consul who died opposing one-man rule would have written. That plausibility is doing all the work: the name supplies the authority, and nobody checks a name that fits.
This is the ordinary shape of a magnet attribution. A line has to sound like its supposed author before it can stick to them — and sounding right is the one property that carries no evidence at all.
detailsBody: If you have a dated citation — a book, an article, a speech, in any language — that predates the modern quotation sites, we would genuinely like to see it. This page will be updated the moment the sentence can be pinned to a source, and its current answer is a report of the state of the evidence rather than a verdict on what is knowable.
context.pull: Sounding like Cicero is not evidence of being Cicero.
